newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq opens way for oil-food deal; U.S. approves.
newsitem.headline: Iraq opens way for oil-food deal; U.S. approves.

text.p: Iraq said on Monday it had agreed to all U.N. conditions for carrying out a delayed "oil-for-food" deal and predicted oil could start flowing some time in December.

"All the aspects of the MOU (memorandum of understanding, or agreement) have been discussed and they have been agreed upon," Iraqi U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon said after a meeting with Undersecretary-General Chinmaya Gharekhan, who heads a U.N. task force overseeing the accord.
American U.N. envoy Madeleine Albright said the United States was "very pleased" and that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali appeared ready to put the deal into effect.
She also said the United States expected to approve an oil pricing formula covering Iraqi oil contracts when it goes before the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee.

This is one of the last steps before implementation of the agreement signed by Iraq and the United Nations in May to permit Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis.
The aim is to ease the effect on ordinary Iraqis of tough U.N. economic sanctions imposed on Iraq since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.

"We are prepared to be able to act positively," Albright told reporters. "We really have good news today ... it is especially good news for the people of Iraq and it is good news for the United States."

Implementation of the "oil-for-food" deal has been delayed due to differences over how it should be carried out, including Iraqi insistence on controlling the number, makeup and freedom of movement of U.N. observers who would monitor arrangements on the ground.
The United Nations also postponed deploying observers after Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq in late August to support one side in an inter-Kurdish conflict.

Referring to an April 1995 Security Council resolution on which the oil-for-food scheme is based, Albright said: "Apparently the secretary-general (Boutros-Ghali) is ready to go forward with implementation of (resolution) 986 because of an agreement by the Iraqis to abide by the memorandum of understanding ... Iraq has now stopped delaying it."
Asked whether the security situation in northern Iraq was no longer an impediment, she said that was a matter to be determined by Boutros-Ghali.
When Hamdoon was asked when Iraqi oil might begin to flow, he replied: "December, I think, is the most likely time for the oil to start moving, because there is nothing else to impede the process."

"I met Mr. Gharekhan and told him Iraq has agreed to implement the memorandum of understanding according to the modalities that were discussed between both sides in the last, I would say, couple of months," Hamdoon said. He had given Gharekhan a letter setting out "the official Iraqi acceptance" of the terms for the deal, he added.
Iraq last week submitted a pricing formula for December to U.N. oil overseers who were to pass it on to the sanctions committee later on Monday with their observations.
The United States delayed committee approval of formulas for previous months, saying other problems must first be worked out.
U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa quoted Boutros-Ghali as saying: "I am optimistic we will have movement within the next few weeks."

She said the United Nations would have to send experts back to northern Iraq to check that oil metering equipment on the Iraq-Turkish border, which had not been in working order, was functioning properly. The bulk of the Iraqi oil was due to flow through a pipeline to Turkey, with the rest being exported via the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr.
Hamdoon said the pipeline to Turkey "will definitely be ready by the first week of December."
"If the pricing formula is approved -- which we hope to get this week -- then nothing else remains," he said.
